Consult Summary:
- Acute gastroenteritis with dehydration suspected after 3 days of watery diarrhea following initial vomiting; management focused on hydration, symptomatic relief, and return-to-work guidance.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Several days of diarrhoea with prior vomiting; now frequent, watery stools.
- Onset and duration: Symptoms began ~3 days ago.
- Course: Vomiting occurred initially and has ceased; diarrhoea persists with about 5–6 stools per day and dehydration symptoms.
- Associated symptoms: Reduced appetite; feeling very dehydrated; weakness; low-grade warmth/fever earlier, currently afebrile; no abdominal pain reported; no blood in stool.
- Exposures/triggers: No clear trigger identified; no recent takeaway or dodgy restaurant food recalled; no sick contacts noted.
- Hydration/oral intake: Struggles to drink enough; ongoing poor fluid intake with ongoing symptomatic diarrhoea.
- Diet: Eats little; not feeling much appetite.
- Other symptoms: No headaches or muscle pains; vomiting has resolved.
- Past medical history: Asthma (infrequent use of blue inhaler).
- Medications: Inhaled blue (short-acting) inhaler; no other medications documented. Dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Social history: Lives alone; software engineer; not a smoker; drinks alcohol socially; off work due to illness.
- Family history: Father had bowel cancer (died ~10 years ago); mother has type 2 diabetes.
- Review of systems: Notable for dehydration; no significant fever currently; no blood in stool; no severe abdominal pain.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Acute gastroenteritis with dehydration, most consistent with a viral gastroenteritis pattern per history; dehydration due to poor oral intake and ongoing diarrhoea.

DDx Integration (top 2–3 aligned with transcript; evidence in brief):
- Viral gastroenteritis (supporting: vomiting initially, then watery diarrhoea; short ~3-day course; dehydration with poor intake; no blood in stool).
  - Opposing signs: prior mild fever noted; not specific to virus but can occur.
- Dehydration/electrolyte disturbances secondary to diarrhoeal illness (supporting: multiple daily loose stools; dehydration signs; weakness; reduced intake).
  - Opposing signs: vitals/labs not provided to quantify dehydration.
- Bacterial gastroenteritis (supporting: acute diarrhoea) 
  - Opposing signs: no documented fever/systemic illness or clear food exposure; no blood in stool.

- Note: No evidence in transcript for inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer as acute presentations; family history of bowel cancer noted but presentation is acute and self-limited.

Issue 1: Acute gastroenteritis with dehydration
- Diagnosis/Impression: Likely viral gastroenteritis with dehydration; self-limited course expected in 3–5 days.
- Plan:
  - Hydration: Encourage high fluid intake; use Dioralyte oral rehydration solution to replenish electrolytes and fluids.
  - Symptom relief: Paracetamol as needed for fever/weakness.
  - Work/activities: Continue to stay off work for next day or two; return to work only after being diarrhoea-free for 24–48 hours.
  - Follow-up: If not better next week, schedule a follow-up appointment.
  - Diet: Small, tolerable meals as appetite returns.
  - Return precautions: Seek urgent care if there is blood in stool, high fever, severe dehydration, inability to keep fluids down, or worsening symptoms.

Issue 2: Asthma (stable/under control)
- Diagnosis/Impression: Chronic asthma; no acute asthma exacerbation documented.
- Plan:
  - Continue current inhaler (blue inhaler) as needed.
  - No changes to asthma management at this visit.
  - Advise returning or seeking care if respiratory symptoms worsen.

Issue 3: Safety-netting and follow-up
- Plan:
  - If symptoms persist or worsen, or if not back to baseline by next week, return for re-evaluation.
  - Monitor hydration status; consider urgent care if signs of dehydration worsen.
  - If new red flags develop (e.g., fever persisting above baseline, blood in stool, severe abdominal pain, inability to keep fluids down), seek urgent evaluation.

General plan items:
- No additional labs or imaging ordered at this time.
- Education provided on oral rehydration and when to seek care.
- Documentation of current medications and allergies reviewed.
